summary: Documents SLIP, Serial Line IP, a widely used de facto way to carry IP over point-to-point serial connections, since there was no standard for serial lines. The RFC itself says it is not an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Serial Line IP (SLIP) frames IP packets for transmission over a serial connection. It uses special bytes to mark packet endings and escape those bytes when they occur in packet data.

subtitle: A simple way to mark packet boundaries on a serial line.

tldr.problem: IP had defined ways to travel over several network types, but no standard framing for plain serial lines even though IP was already being used on them.
tldr.mechanism: SLIP sends packet bytes and marks the end with END. It substitutes two-byte escape sequences when an END or ESC byte occurs inside the packet.
tldr.outcome: SLIP provides packet framing only; it has no addressing, protocol-type field, error detection, or compression. The RFC calls it a de facto protocol, not an Internet standard.

facts.label: Status stated in RFC text
facts.value: De facto, not an Internet standard

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 1055 as an Internet Standard. The RFC's own text describes SLIP as a de facto protocol and says it is not an Internet standard.

sections.title: Why SLIP Was Used
sections.content:
TCP/IP ran over many media, including Ethernet, token ring, X.25, satellite links, and serial lines. Standard packet encapsulations existed for many of those media, but not for serial lines. SLIP filled that gap as a de facto framing protocol for point-to-point serial connections.

The RFC describes SLIP as a small protocol that frames IP packets and nothing more. It explicitly says that SLIP is not an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: SLIP provided a way to mark IP packets on a serial line where no standard framing method was available. It did not define a full network protocol.

sections.title: How SLIP Spread
sections.content:
SLIP originated in the 3COM UNET TCP/IP implementation in the early 1980s. Around 1984, Rick Adams implemented it for 4.2 Berkeley Unix and Sun Microsystems workstations and released it.

The RFC describes use on dedicated serial links and sometimes dialup connections, including host-to-host, host-to-router, and router-to-router links. It notes typical line speeds from 1200bps to 19.2Kbps and says implementations were available for Berkeley-derived Unix systems and some other platforms.
sections.plainLanguage: SLIP spread because it was small and straightforward to implement. The RFC records its use on dedicated and dialup serial links.

sections.title: How SLIP Marks Packet Boundaries
sections.content:
SLIP defines END as octal 300 (decimal 192) and ESC as octal 333 (decimal 219). A sender transmits the packet bytes and then an END byte. If data contains END, the sender transmits ESC followed by octal 334; if data contains ESC, it transmits ESC followed by octal 335.

The RFC describes an optional initial END byte to flush bytes left by line noise. It suggests accepting packets up to 1006 bytes, including IP and transport headers but excluding framing bytes, as used by Berkeley UNIX drivers.
sections.plainLanguage: An END byte marks a packet's boundary. When that byte or ESC appears as data, SLIP replaces it with a two-byte escape sequence.

sections.title: The Reference Send and Receive Functions
sections.content:
The RFC includes C functions that send and receive SLIP packets. The sender adds an initial END, escapes END and ESC bytes inside the packet, and sends a final END. The receiver reads until END and reverses the escape sequences.

The receiver ignores an END when it has received no packet data, avoiding an empty packet after consecutive END bytes. If ESC is followed by an unrecognized byte, the example treats the byte as data. A packet longer than the receiver's buffer is truncated.
sections.plainLanguage: The example sender adds boundary markers and escapes special data bytes. The receiver reads to the next marker and reverses those substitutions.

sections.title: What SLIP Does Not Provide
sections.content:
SLIP has no way to communicate IP addresses, identify different network protocols, detect or correct damaged packets, or compress data. The two computers must already know each other's IP addresses, and only one protocol can use a SLIP connection.

The RFC notes that line noise can corrupt packets and that retransmission may be expensive on slow links. It says various groups were working on a successor that would address some or all of these shortcomings.
sections.plainLanguage: SLIP marks packet boundaries but does not identify hosts or detect packet damage. It also cannot carry multiple network protocols or compress packet data.
